questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061629/assets/78f8ca3e70afb8377748a18d7024ba297e330add59550a41a87025a0145b56bb.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}9xy\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$  traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}9xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =2(8-1) \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+49{y}^{2}=196,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{7}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $7$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{49{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{45{sin}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{45{sin}^{2}⁡t+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{2(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=7\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }7\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{45{sin}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{45{sin}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061629/assets/0b0f3ae9a464812957c297c09ff3f65bfe5964bdac70298e72ec3dbde2325e72.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(6{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the right half of the ellipse $6{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=6,$ shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $\sqrt{6},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=6{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-6{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(6{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=4xy$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+8{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $\sqrt{2},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡t+2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{2+2{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=4xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t=8\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}4xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{2+2{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{2+2{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2+2{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{2+2{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{2}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{2}^{2} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061629/assets/9684a8beb9981ac024d56d7467672b66c73eeb90c8dcaae11e61c0686dc1fcde.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(4x-2y)\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $4,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{12{cos}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{12{cos}^{2}⁡t+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=4x-2y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-2(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡t-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =8(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(4x-2y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }8(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
